pr_body:
Implemented fix that pushes updated timestamps to previous version, in the case that no files were changed, and no new backup is recorded in remote storage.

This fixes #4312

issue_context.title: Backup not saved if only metadata has changed
issue_context.body:
<!-- Thank you for taking the time to submit an issue using this template. By following the instructions and filling out the sections below, you will help the developers get the necessary information to fix your issue. You may remove sections that aren't relevant to your particular case. You can also preview your report before submitting it. -->
<!-- Love Duplicati? Please consider supporting our collective at https://opencollective.com/duplicati/donate. -->

<!-- Please search to see if an issue has already been created for your report. -->
<!-- Replace the empty checkbox [ ] below with a checked one [x] if you already searched for duplicate bugs. -->
- [x] I have searched open and closed issues for duplicates.

----------------------------------------

## Environment info
<!-- Please include some relevant information about your environment. -->
<!-- For "Backend", please indicate the backup destination (e.g. Amazon S3, OneDrive, FTP, WebDAV, local). -->
- **Duplicati version**: 2.0.5.1_beta_2020-01-18
- **Operating system**: Linux in a docker container
- **Backend**: Jottacloud

## Description
<!-- Describe the issue that you are experiencing below. -->
After deleting and recreating the local database, subsequent backups with unchanged files showed the Duplicati was 'opening' a significant number of files, despite no changes having been made. Further investigation showed that this was because Duplicati thought that the timestamps had changed on those files, although logging showed that the timestamps were actually the same (presumably some sort of precision difference). However, despite Duplicati checking these files, it presumably did not update the timestamps in the database, meaning that subsequent backups would still 'open' these files. This meant that a backup run would take well over an hour, instead of just a couple of minutes.

The issue was 'resolved' by adding an empty file into the backup set, forcing Duplicati to retain the backup it made, and update the file metadata.

## Steps to reproduce
<!-- List the steps to reproduce the bug if possible. -->
1. Delete and recreate the database
2. Run a backup having made no changes to the backup set, observe lots of files being 'opened'
3. Repeat the backup, again having made no changes to the backup set. Again, lots of files being 'opened'

<!-- For "Actual result", describe what happens after you run the steps above (i.e. buggy behavior). -->
<!-- For "Expected result", describe what should happen after you run the steps above (i.e. corrected behavior). -->
- **Actual result**:
Lots of files in the backup set being opened and read, despite no changes having been made to them
- **Expected result**:
Unchanged files should be immediately skipped by the backup

## Debug log
Lots of entries visible like the following:

```Checking file for changes <redacted>, new: False, timestamp changed: True, size changed: False, metadatachanged: False, 9/4/2020 1:07:47 PM vs 9/4/2020 1:07:47 PM```
comments:
This issue has been mentioned on **Duplicati**. There might be relevant details there:

https://forum.duplicati.com/t/after-deleting-and-recreating-database-backup-is-opening-files-un-necessarily/10700/10

Ok well this is interesting.  I spent some time digging into this.

During a database recreation, the timestamps are restored to the FilelsetEntry db table from filelist.json in each dlist file.  These timestamps have precision only to the second, ie: 20200911T031433Z.  Normally when Duplicati does backups it records a more precise timestamp to the database.

Duplicati also restores metadata hashes and file content hashes from the same filelist.json files during a database recreation.

These timestamps are part of the metadata hash.  You'd think that the first backup after a database recreate would detect a difference in metadata hash, but it doesn't. When Duplicati scans the actual files and recomputes the metadata hash, it matches the correctly restored hash value - even though in reality the timestamp as recorded in the database is different (less precise) than the timestamp it read from the filesystem.

Duplicati detects this timestamp difference during the backup operation, which forces a rescan of the file contents.  But unless the file contents have changed, the file content hashes will match.  And the metadata hashes match as well as discussed in the previous paragraph.  The net result is Duplicati doesn't think this file really changed (even though the timestamp is different!) -- It's not counted when Duplicati checks for the number of changed files in this backup set:

https://github.com/duplicati/duplicati/blob/master/Duplicati/Library/Main/Database/LocalBackupDatabase.cs#L607

As a result the backup set may be deleted (if AddedFiles+DeletedFiles+ModifiedFiles = 0).

Possible ways to fix this issue:
* Increase time resolution in the dlist filelist.json files to match what is really recorded in the database.
* Adjust the line in the above quoted code to also compare timestamps.
* If a rescan of ALL file contents is a good idea after database recreation, maybe don't restore the metadata hash during a recreation.  This would force a full rescan of file contents but Duplicati would definitely not drop this backup set because it would detect the metadata hash differences.

Also - directory timestamps aren't recorded in filelist.json so their value in the database after a recreate is basically 0.  Should directory timestamps be recorded in filelist.json?

I experimented with option 1 - increasing resolution of time stored in filelist.json.  It seems to solve the issue.  now when i do a database recreation, the timestamp is restored with full resolution and on the next backup Duplicati doesn't feel the need to scan the file contents.

What happens if the more precise filelist.json is read by a current Duplicati? It should work no worse than a low-res filelist.json.
Same concern for [Duplicati.CommandLine.RecoveryTool.exe](https://duplicati.readthedocs.io/en/latest/07-other-command-line-utilities/#duplicaticommandlinerecoverytoolexe), [restore_from_python.py](https://forum.duplicati.com/t/independent-restore-program/2316), and utility-scripts DuplicatiVerify.{ps1,py}.

I'm not sure what you use to read FilesetEntry `Lastmodified`, but [.NET DateTime Ticks Converter Online](https://www.venea.net/web/net_ticks_datetime_converter#net_ticks_to_date_time_and_unix_timestamp_conversion) seems to do the job.

I'd be interested to know the original reason for using that one second resolution timestamp in the format for the backup files.
This seems to potentially lead to making [disaster recovery](https://duplicati.readthedocs.io/en/latest/08-disaster-recovery/) timestamps a bit low (small price to pay compared to file contents)...

Looks like older versions would not be able to process the increased time resolution, so it would cause issues downgrading.  If we had to avoid such a scenario, we could do something clunky like store the higher res part of the timestamp in a different property in the json.

I don't know the history of time resolution in .NET, but I recall mono 5.x having higher res support than the older versions. Some noticed their files getting rescanned after upgrading mono, because Duplicati detected a difference in timestamp.

Not sure what Duplicati really needs to support.  If high res is needed, then I think we should improve how it's stored in the json.  If second-level resolution is fine, then we could perhaps try my second idea.
Anyone else have any thoughts on this?  After I did a database recreation on one of my backup sets, I was reminded of this issue.

Is the suggestion to change the following line to store more precision?

https://github.com/duplicati/duplicati/blob/9b977b7ba04a940868754fd15a37b99fbd77f1bd/Duplicati/Library/Utility/Utility.cs#L981

When deserializing, could we maintain backward compatibility by determining the serialization format based on the length of the string?

Exactly the approach I tested a month ago.  I created a "high res" format constant of:  `yyyyMMdd'T'HHmmssfffffffK`
During deserialization, it would first try the high res format.  If that failed, it tries the current "low res" format.  If that failed as well, an exception is thrown.  This maintains compatibility with older filelist.json files nicely.

The main problem with this approach is if a user were to downgrade Duplicati.  Older versions do not handle the "high res" timestamps at all, so they will fail when processing them.  One possible solution is to store the high res timestamp in a different variable in the json.  Older versions would just ignore it.

Two other ideas which may or may not be good ones...

If you have file metadata (not guaranteed, given [skip-metadata](https://duplicati.readthedocs.io/en/latest/06-advanced-options/#skip-metadata)) it looks like it has a timestamp without artificial precision loss in the formatting. Examples [here](https://github.com/duplicati/duplicati/blob/a80d50687eab27e0308581178ad618878bfbcb85/Duplicati/Library/Main/Operation/Backup/MetadataGenerator.cs#L48-L58) and [here](https://github.com/duplicati/duplicati/blob/a80d50687eab27e0308581178ad618878bfbcb85/Duplicati/Library/Main/Operation/RestoreHandler.cs#L529-L535). I suspect usually you have metadata, but it has to still work if you don't. It's also probably a bit slower to dig out of the data, and I'm not sure if it's even available at the right time. Example from a metadata block from Windows:

> {"win-ext:accessrules":"[]","CoreAttributes":"Archive","CoreLastWritetime":"637373725585437959","CoreCreatetime":"637280032769823521"}

[upload-unchanged-backups](https://duplicati.readthedocs.io/en/latest/06-advanced-options/#upload-unchanged-backups) does a good job of forcing the new-resolution timestamps out (even if no data content changes happen for the [change count-and-check code](https://github.com/duplicati/duplicati/blob/a80d50687eab27e0308581178ad618878bfbcb85/Duplicati/Library/Main/Operation/Backup/UploadRealFilelist.cs#L47-L55)). While one could add more statistics for timestamp changes, maybe there could be a flag kept to remember, and force a version. The downside of that is source files get scanned, but full scan does help ensure the backup is right.

A somewhat exotic problem that a full-resolution timestamp will still run into is that some filesystems and file transfer methods may lose precision. I think there are still 1-second resolution filesystems around that may still think times "changed" from the hi-res ones.

I haven't looked at the code now, but from the database I suspect we're talking about the FilesetEntry table Lastmodified ticks here... That's what I was seeing lose sub-second precision on Recreate, and make me look for ways to get the full prevision back somehow...

> it looks like it has a timestamp without artificial precision loss

It's stored in the database with full precision, but not stored in filelist.json (in the dlist files) with full precision.  So when the database is rebuilt from back end files, precision is lost.  This loss of precision is detected and forces a full rescan of files.

Forcing a version after database recreation is an interesting idea, and is one way to "solve" the issue.  But it seems more correct to me to store full timestamp precision in the dlist files.

> It's stored in the database with full precision, but not stored in filelist.json (in the dlist files) with full precision. So when the database is rebuilt from back end files, precision is lost.

The point was that typical back end files store full precision timestamp in easy format in metadata now, so rebuild "could" get that,
however it might not be as convenient for the code. The dlist file seems an easy one-stop grab, compared to peeking in metadata.

> But it seems more correct to me to store full timestamp precision in the dlist files.

I think I prefer this plan (provided all tools support it, and keeping in mind that full timestamp might still not be possible to store).

One nagging worry is why it wasn't done at high precision originally, since it looks easy (at least now) to ask for it in format string.
If I follow the .NET plan, this would use [The "fffffff" custom format specifier](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/base-types/custom-date-and-time-format-strings#fffffffSpecifier). The uppercase F version looks like it "might" read back seconds with or without the 0000000 fractional precision, "determining the serialization format based on the length of the string" provided the choices are either full precision or even seconds. I didn't spot one that just filled in trailing 0s for whatever it needed, although I'm not an expert and haven't tested code. Possibly Duplicati was developed on a system with just 1 second FS precision. [HFS+](https://discussions.apple.com/thread/7973917) would have been that way.  [ext3](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/60841940/file-timestamps-precision-ext3-with-nanoseconds-ext4-with-milliseconds) may vary depending on inode sizes. [FAT32](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File_Allocation_Table#FAT32) at 2 second precision suggests loss is survivable.

> The point was that typical back end files store full precision timestamp in easy format in metadata now, so rebuild "could" get that,

Oh I see what you mean. I think that metadata info is stored in the dblocks, right?  Having to read dblocks during database recreation is a pretty big downside to that approach.

> The uppercase F version looks like it "might" read back seconds with or without the 0000000 fractional precision

I'll test it out and let you know.  This would be nice if true, BUT it still doesn't help people who may need to downgrade Duplicati.  Higher res timestamps will still cause issues on existing versions.

The uppercase F indeed seems to work better than lower case f.  Unlike `yyyyMMdd'T'HHmmssfffffffK`, the format string `yyyyMMdd'T'HHmmssFFFFFFFK` also works when those digits are missing (as you speculated, @ts678).  This simplifies things a lot since we don't have to try both formats.

Unfortunately, it still doesn't help people who decide to downgrade Duplicati.  The higher time precision in filelist.json will confuse older versions of Duplicati.  If we want to avoid changes that block downgrades, we could store the sub-second part of the time resolution in a separate field in the json.  Kind of messy, but won't cause downgrade issues.  Thoughts?

> Having to read dblocks during database recreation is a pretty big downside to that approach.

I agree it's probably not feasible. I haven't looked at code, but typically all you want to download is dlist and dindex.

> If we want to avoid changes that block downgrades

I would prefer not making downgrades worse than they already are, however I don't know how everybody else feels.
Putting an incompatible format into the dlist files seems a more permanent problem than usual DB versioning pains.
Super-ugly way to try revert might use [Repair command deletes remote files for new backups #3416](https://github.com/duplicati/duplicati/issues/3416) to advantage,..
I wouldn't seriously suggest it, especially because compacts might have completely rearranged the destination files...

Having disposed of dubious alternatives, I don't know if there's a better method than storing sub-second separately.

@warwickmm it's been a month since I was delving into this, so my memory may be rusty.  But from what I recall here's the scenario:

After a database recreation, the timestamps restored to the new database are lower res. The metadata hashes are restored properly.

During the next backup, Duplicati detects that timestamps don't match the filesystem timestamp (because of different resolution) and forces a full reprocessing of the source files.  Regarding the metadata hash, Duplicati calculates a new metadata hash based on the active filesystem properties.  This metahash DOES match what was restored during the database recreation.  Because these hashes match, it decides the reprocessed file really isn't different (which is true).  If this happens to ALL reprocessed files, then the  first backup after database recreation isn't kept.  It gets dropped because Duplicati thinks nothing really changed.  The next backup then repeats the process and does the more lengthy "reprocess all file contents" thing.  This keeps happening until at least one file is *actually* changed.  Once that happens the backup set is committed and future backups stop reprocessing existing, unchanged files.

This whole thing is avoided if we can restore full timestamp resolution during a database recreation.  I think adding a "high res" timestamp to the filelist.json would achieve this goal.  I can submit a PR for further review if we have tentative consensus on this approach.
Thanks, I think I understand now.  Please go ahead and submit the pull request when you have time.  Thanks for debugging this!

Well this approach won't work any better from a downgrade point of view.

It seems `FilesetVolumeReader.cs` expects JSON properties to be in a certain order.  Adding a new property would break older versions' ability to process them properly.

> Adjust the line in the above quoted code to also compare timestamps.

Any downsides to modifying the query and documenting in the code why we're comparing metadata _and_ timestamps?

Only downside is that all files would still have to be reprocessed once after a database recreation.  Better than the current situation, but not ideal.  I'm not sure there is a way to implement an ideal fix for this and maintain the ability to allow downgrades.

I'll explore the option of changing the query....
I had some time to explore that option and it didn't take long for me to realize it is beyond my abilities when it comes to SQL.

Another idea - what if when Duplicati is comparing timestamps, it limits it to second-level resolution?  It would ignore any sub-second differences, unless other metadata changes were detected (like file size).

The storing of timestamps in the database can still be full resolution.  File restores would be full resolution if the timestamp in the database is used.

Second-level resolution will match `filelist.json`, therefore it would "solve" the problem caused by database recreation.  (It still feels a bit hacky but I really dislike the idea of introducing downgrade issues...)

> what if when Duplicati is comparing timestamps, it limits it to second-level resolution?

Tested this and it does work.
Is this localized to comparisons against the timestamp in the `filelist.json`?  If so, this approach would make sense given that we know the `filelist.json` timestamp is lower resolution.

Unfortunately no, I'm not sure how you would do it that way.  After database recreation, the timestamps stored in the database are lower res. They aren't compared to filesystem timestamps until the next backup.  At that point Duplicati just compares database timestamp to filesystem timestamp.

What about this compromise: reduce resolution of the database timestamp to filesystem timestamp comparison ONLY when the sub-second timestamp in the database is "0".

I'm not sure what the implications of limiting timestamp comparisons to second-level resolution are.  There may be other places in the code that also require second-level resolution only.  For example, the `RestoreHandler.FilterNumberedFilelist` method (used in both restore and repair operations) explicitly strips milliseconds from the `DateTime`:

https://github.com/duplicati/duplicati/blob/9b977b7ba04a940868754fd15a37b99fbd77f1bd/Duplicati/Library/Main/Operation/RestoreHandler.cs#L69-L71
